shortfall_reason: Filtered pool held 7 items; 3 collapsed under dedup. (1) Books+Publishing 'Princeton University Press partners with Cashmere on AI licensing' is the same story already published 2026-08-04 as card 'books-princeton-cashmere-licensing' (Publishers Weekly framing) -> dropped. (2) The $2.4m crime-novel-pulled-over-AI thread appeared in 3 outlets this window (PW 'After the Cancellation of Call Me, I'll Hide The Body', The Bookseller 'It was inevitable', Books+Publishing 'Agent pulls manuscript from sale'), but the underlying withdrawal already ran 2026-08-01 as card 'genius-novel-pulled' (The Bookseller). Only ONE follow-up was kept, and only because it carries reporting the 08-01 card did not: the agents' collective reaction and the admission that there is no reliable way to authenticate how a manuscript was made. The other two same-event items were dropped. Backfill exhausted the ranked pool, so 4 distinct never-before-seen stories is the honest ceiling -- above the floor of 3, no padding. Diversity guard satisfied: 3 distinct outlets, max 2 per domain (Publishing Perspectives x2), no repeated URL within the final set or against the books section history.

items.title: 'It was inevitable': Agents react to major book deal that collapsed over suspected AI use
items.excerpt: A crime novel that sold for $2.4m in a 14-way US auction was pulled by its agent on 31 July over suspected AI-generated content, and literary agents tell The Bookseller they now have no reliable way to authenticate how a manuscript was made. Agents describe uncertainty and fear becoming the default posture on submission.
items.rationale: The withdrawal itself ran on 08-01, so this card must be framed on the new part -- agents admitting they cannot authenticate how a manuscript was made, which changes how writers submit tomorrow.
items.writer_note: Do NOT retell the book being pulled (already published 2026-08-01 as 'genius-novel-pulled'). Lead on the agents' reaction and the authentication gap.

items.title: Local secondhand booksellers suspect AI companies behind bulk orders
items.excerpt: Secondhand booksellers across Australia and New Zealand report unusual bulk orders from Canadian recycling firm Zoom Books and suspect the stock is feeding AI training pipelines; Zoom Books denies digitising books for generative AI. Shows the physical-book supply chain becoming a training-data acquisition channel.
items.rationale: Fresh and never covered here: training-data acquisition reaching down into used-bookshop inventory, a supply-chain angle no card in this section has touched.

items.title: Around the Book World: August 3, 2026 - agents rewrite their ethics code for the AI era
items.excerpt: The Association of American Literary Agents has revised its Canon of Ethics to cover 'emerging technologies,' effective 1 September 2026; the same roundup notes Korean 20- and 30-somethings reading more as a counterweight to heavy AI use, and Hachette's parent expecting $22m+ from the Anthropic settlement.
items.rationale: A dated, binding rule change (AALA Canon of Ethics, effective 1 September) is the most actionable item in the pool -- it tells authors and agents exactly what conduct is about to be governed.

items.title: Legal Battle Over U.S. Copyright Chief Heats Up Again
items.excerpt: The fight over who runs the U.S. Copyright Office is back in court, and the outcome shapes how the office rules on AI training and AI-assisted authorship registration. Lower-priority for a craft-focused brief, but it is the policy substrate under every AI-and-books story this week.
items.rationale: Newest item in the pool and the policy layer under the week's other stories: whoever runs the Copyright Office decides how AI-assisted authorship gets registered.
